summary.text: An event horizon is a boundary in spacetime beyond which no signal can ever reach a given observer.
The best-known example is a black hole, where inside the horizon every path light could take is warped so that it falls farther into the hole.
Horizons also arise in an expanding universe, where expansion reaching light speed keeps signals from some regions from ever arriving.

facts.label: Inside a black hole
facts.value: Moving inward is as inevitable as moving forward in time

facts.label: Early idea
facts.value: Michell proposed in 1784 that gravity could trap light

facts.label: Seen from outside
facts.value: Approaching objects appear to slow and redden

items.prompt: You watch a probe sink toward a black hole from far away. What do you see as it nears the horizon?

options.label: It speeds up and flashes brighter
It slows, never quite crossing, and its image reddens
It vanishes at once without any trace
It circles at a steady distance

items.explain: Objects approaching the horizon appear to slow down without crossing, and gravitational redshift reddens their image.

items.prompt: Stephen Hawking suggested using apparent horizons rather than event horizons. What was his argument about gravitational collapse?

options.label: It produces apparent horizons but no event horizons
It produces event horizons but no apparent horizons
It produces neither kind of horizon
It produces horizons only for spinning stars

items.explain: Hawking said collapse produces apparent horizons but no event horizons.

items.prompt: A particle is already inside a black hole's event horizon and tries to head in some direction. What is its fate?

options.label: It escapes if it moves outward fast enough
It circles at fixed distance
It stays still forever
Moving inward is as inevitable as moving forward in time

items.explain: Inside the horizon, moving into the hole is as unavoidable as moving forward in time, whatever direction the particle travels.

items.prompt: A popular description says the horizon is where escape velocity exceeds light's speed. What is the more detailed picture?

options.label: Light there simply runs out of energy
Light paths there are bent so they all fall farther in
Matter there becomes infinitely dense
Time there is perfectly uniform

items.explain: Within the horizon, all lightlike paths are warped so as to fall farther into the hole.

items.prompt: An idealized rocket accelerates uniformly forever. What does its crew find about events behind it?

options.label: They eventually see every event
They see events only in slow motion
A boundary behind them that signals never cross
Time for them seems to run backward

items.explain: An accelerating particle gets an apparent horizon, a boundary beyond which events can never be observed.

items.prompt: A particle coasts at constant velocity in a non-expanding universe with no gravity. Will it eventually be able to observe every event?

options.label: No, distant events stay hidden forever
Yes, light from every event eventually reaches it
Only if it speeds up at some point
Only the events that lie behind it

items.explain: Forward light cones from the events cross a constant-velocity particle's world line, so each event is eventually observable.
